summary: A 1931 Aermotor tower on South Beacon Mountain; retired from fire watch in the 1970s or 1980s, listed 2009, restored by volunteers and reopened to hikers June 2013.

facts.design: Aermotor LS-40 steel tower, 60 ft, with a 7 x 7 ft metal cab and 72 steps

staffing.status: not staffed; the last assigned fire ranger was in 1972

access.note: Described as a hiking destination and reopened to hikers in 2013; the tower remains a DEC tower on City of Beacon land. Scenic Hudson's page is undated, so check current conditions before going.

visit.trail_note: Strenuous hike, less than a mile from the North Mount Beacon summit, per Scenic Hudson.

events.note: Observer post listed as South Beacon Mtn. before any tower; the observer walked down a foot trail to a phone line
Aermotor LS-40 erected on the site of an earlier wooden tower
Began supporting fire observation in the area
Last assigned fire ranger in 1972; taken out of active service at the end of the 1972 observation season
Historic Structures says the tower was briefly back in service, then decommissioned permanently around 1975
NHLR says the tower was decommissioned in 1987 (sources disagree with c. 1975)
Restoration interest first initiated; a formal organizing meeting with NYSDEC, the City of Beacon and others took place
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register December 16, 2005 as US 655
Replacement steps installed over the summer of 2008
Added to the National Register of Historic Places October 23, 2009 (ref. 09000862)
Restoration completed with volunteers and the New York Army National Guard; tower reopened June 22, 2013 with a ceremony

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR says decommissioned in 1987 after 50 years of use; Historic Structures says the tower was taken out of active service after the 1972 season, briefly returned, and was permanently decommissioned around 1975; the restoration group says five decades of use. The story reports the disagreement and does not pick a single year.
NHLR gives 1,600 ft (488 m), which matches the record; Scenic Hudson gives a 1,610-foot peak and the restoration group gives 1,650 ft. The record keeps the NHLR value.

notes_for_editor: The 1931 build date is consistent across four sources. The retirement date conflicts: NHLR says 1987, Historic Structures says permanently decommissioned around 1975 after a brief return to service; the NHLR's 50-year claim and the restoration group's five decades match neither the 1932-1972 observation dates. The record's access 'unknown' is replaced with public on hiking-destination evidence, but the Scenic Hudson page is undated and current access was not checked against a live source. The 2009 NRHP date comes from Wikipedia, which cites the NPS weekly list. The 'restoration now completed' wording is from Historic Structures and is undated. The record's 2005 NHLR registration and the 18.3 m height are correct. No new photos were added.
